amendments.rule: Inside a compound numeral the English juncture *and* has no Greek counterpart but is obligatory idiom, so it is a helper and not `added`: attach each *and* to the numeral token it introduces, and keep the numerals themselves separate even when the ASV reorders them. `ἑκατὸν τεσσεράκοντα τέσσαρες χιλιάδες` → *a hundred*, *and forty*, *and four*, *thousand*, each headed on its numeral; `εἴκοσι τέσσαρες` → *four* for `τέσσαρες` and *and twenty* for `εἴκοσι`, headed on *twenty*. That separation is scoped to where the ASV writes a word for each numeral, and it is not a licence to split one English word across them. Where the ASV compresses a compound numeral into a **single** English word, the numeral tokens and any `καί` standing between them are one `aligned` unit taking that word, headed on the token the word's stem realizes: `δέκα καὶ ὀκτὼ ἔτη` → *eighteen years* gives *eighteen* to the three tokens headed on `ὀκτώ`, and *years* to the noun. Rule 94's count test is what decides it, the count of English words the ASV wrote being the test there as here, and rule 39's test keeps the unit `aligned` rather than `noncompositional`, *eight-* answering to `ὀκτώ` and *-teen* to `δέκα`. The intervening `καί` is neither `added` nor `unrepresented`: this rule's own reason holds, an obligatory English juncture inside one numeral idiom belonging to the idiom, and here the idiom is spelt solid. Do not leave any member of such a compound empty in order to give the single word to one of them alone. Where the Greek writes the compound as one token the question does not arise and the unit is an ordinary one-to-one alignment, as `δεκαοκτώ` → *eighteen* is.
amendments.why: Rule 29's sentence 'keep the numerals themselves separate even when the ASV reorders them' was written for renderings that spell each numeral out, and every example it carries is one. LUK.13.16 met the case it had not considered: δέκα καὶ ὀκτώ rendered by the single word *eighteen*, where separation is not merely wrong but impossible, one target token being unable to belong to three units. Read first, the unamended rule sends a later pass either to an unmakeable partition or to emptying δέκα and καί against the rule's own refusal to leave a juncture unrepresented. The added clause fires only where the ASV wrote one word, which none of rule 29's own examples does, so it takes nothing away from them; rules 39, 50 and 94 already decide every other one-English-word compression the same way (ἕως ἂν → *till*, οὐ δύναται → *cannot*, οὐδὲ ἕν → *nothing*), and the same chapter joins ἕως ὅτου and ἕως οὗ on *till* by that test. The head goes on ὀκτώ as the word's stem element, with the note at LUK.13.16 recording that assigning the whole word to ὀκτώ while emptying the other two was the competing reading.

conventions: ἀφ' οὗ is decided on the English by rule 45's test, not on the Greek phrase: at 13:7 the ASV writes *these*, which answers to neither token, so the pair is one `noncompositional` unit; at 13:25 it writes *When*, which answers to the relative, so the same pair is one `aligned` unit. Both are headed on the governed word. This is rule 45's own ἐν ᾧ → *wherewith* against *while*, and a chapter writing both is following rule 24's habit.

ἕως with a following relative compressed into a single English word is one `aligned` unit headed on ἕως, by rule 94's count test and rule 39's status test: ἕως ὅτου → *till* at 13:8 and ἕως οὗ → *till* at 13:21. A bare ἕως keeps its own word in the ordinary way, as ἕως → *until* does at 13:35.

εἰ δὲ μήγε at 13:9 is split token by token — δέ → *but*, εἰ → *if*, μήγε → *not* — because the ASV wrote three English words. Rule 39's cluster is scoped to a rendering by one English word, which is what the corpus's *else* and *or else* units (LUK.5.36, LUK.5.37, JHN.14.11, REV.2.5) all carry; do not join the cluster mechanically from those precedents where the ASV has spelled it out.

συκῆ → *fig tree* is headed on *tree* at 13:6 and 13:7, *tree* being what glosses the lexeme and *fig* the specifying modifier (rule 66's first arm). A head on *fig*, on the analogy of ἀγάπαις → *love feasts*, remains defensible and is what the 13:6 note names.

A compound agent noun rendered by two words each glossing an element is headed by rule 66's morphological core and never by the English phrase's formal head: ἀρχισυνάγωγος → *ruler of the synagogue* heads on *synagogue* at 13:14, as πιθανολογίᾳ → *persuasiveness of speech* heads on *speech*, and οἰκοδεσπότης → *master of the house* heads on *master* at 13:25, δεσπότης being that compound's core. The two land on opposite English positions under one test. A head on *ruler* at 13:14 remains the competing reading and would rest on English syntax alone.

Where the Greek verb has no expressed object and the ASV writes a single negative word carrying both the clause's negation and the object English requires, that word is the negator's own `aligned` unit and the verb stands on its own word: οὐχ εὗρεν → *found* and *none* at 13:6, οὐχ εὑρίσκω → *find* and *none* at 13:7. Rules 41 and 59 do not empty the negator here, no second negative token standing; the supplied pronominal rides inside the negator's unit as a rule 7 helper.

report: Read all 56 candidate groups and the verse dump end to end, including the added units the lemma table is blind to. No construction is analysed two ways without a difference in the source or in the ASV's own wording to license it, so no patch is returned.

Near-misses examined and cleared. ἀφ' οὗ is noncompositional at 13:7 (*these*, answering to neither token) and aligned at 13:25 (*When*, answering to the relative); rule 45 names exactly this shape for ἐν ᾧ → *wherewith* against *while*, so the English decides and this is one analysis, not two. ἕως ὅτου (13:8) and ἕως οὗ (13:21) are joined identically on *till*. δεῖ leaves the supplied infinitival subject on the infinitive at 13:14 and aligns the expressed accusative subject με at 13:33 — rule 74, and the Greek differs. εἰς is aligned at 13:19 s009 and unrepresented at s016 because *became a tree* writes no preposition (rule 36's predicate-absorption clause). εἰ is aligned at 13:9 inside a three-word cluster and unrepresented at 13:23, where the ASV recasts the indirect question as a direct one and writes no word.

Applied uniformly and consistently across the chapter: rule 38 empties the article before an attributive demonstrative at 13:2, 13:4, 13:6, 13:7, 13:8, 13:16 and 13:32; rules 20 and 76 divide the supplied possessive the same way at 13:15 and 13:34, each of which writes both arms in one verse, with 13:6, 13:12, 13:17, 13:26 and 13:35 on the rule 20 side; rule 88 puts the supplied juncture on the finite verb it introduces at 13:2, 13:14, 13:19, 13:21, 13:25 and 13:32; rule 102 gives the supplied *day* to the article at both 13:32 and 13:33; rule 106 keeps every preverb particle inside its verb and keeps the preposition of an accusative object there too (13:4 *dwell in*, 13:25 *knock at*); rule 89 folds every supplied address word onto an anarthrous vocative at 13:15, 13:27 and 13:34.

The three added units carry no counterpart that was folded instead. 13:9 *well* and 13:16 *these* are supplied where no token stands at all, and 13:34 *gathereth* is rule 103's resumed verb, ἐπισυνάξαι being spent on *gathered*. The italicized words that were folded — *day* at 13:32 and 13:33 onto the article under rule 102, *is* at 13:35 onto the predicate participle — each have a token whose English was still incomplete, and 13:35 *desolate* aligns to ἔρημος, which the selected reading r01 of SBLGNT.LUK.13.35.v034 puts in the projection. So the licensing test, not italics, decided every one.

BSB: all five disagreements are documented convention differences and none is an error. 13:9 τὸ and 13:11 τὸ are articles the ASV writes no determiner for (rules 93 and 23); 13:19 εἰς is absorbed into *became a tree*, which rule 36 names in terms; 13:23 εἰ has no English word answering to it once the question is recast as direct; 13:28 τῶν stands before the determinerless *of teeth* (rules 23 and 21). Nothing was changed to move the figure.

Recorded six conventions and one amendment. The amendment narrows rule 29, which as written would have a later pass split δέκα / καί / ὀκτώ across the single English word *eighteen* at 13:16 — a partition that cannot be made.
